name: The lord on whose hand the king leaned
charge: Scoffing at the word of the Lord by Elisha in the famine of Samaria
summary: In a siege so hard that women ate their children, Elisha said that by the next day fine flour would sell for a shekel in the gate. The king's officer answered that it could not happen if the Lord opened windows in heaven. He saw it, and was trampled in the gate by the crowd rushing to buy.
offense: Samaria's famine had reached extremity when Elisha declared that flour and barley would be sold cheaply at the gate the next day. The officer upon whose hand the king leaned answered by asking whether such a thing could happen even if the Lord made windows in heaven (2 Kings 7:1-2). Present scarcity became his measure of what the Lord could provide. The promise did not require him to explain the means before believing the word. His answer treated the announcement as impossible at the moment it was expressly given in the Lord's name. A trusted position beside the king did not supply understanding of a deliverance neither man had arranged.
judgment: Elisha told him that he would see the abundance but not eat it. The Lord caused the Syrians to hear a host approaching, and they fled, leaving their provisions behind. Four leprous men discovered the empty camp and reported it (2 Kings 7:3-11). Relief came through a means the officer had not included in his objection. The people spoiled the camp, and the prices fell as announced. Appointed to oversee the gate, the officer was trampled there and died (2 Kings 7:16-20). The place where the promised provision became publicly available was the place where his exclusion was fulfilled. He witnessed the answer his unbelief had dismissed, but did not share its food.

entries.commentary: Elisha declares the word of the Most High that within a day the famine will break and fine flour and barley will sell cheaply in the gate of Samaria. The lord on whose hand the king leaned doubts the word, asking if the Most High would make windows in heaven. Elisha tells him he will see it with his eyes but not eat of it. The prophet speaks the word of the Most High plainly, without fear and without doubting, whether the message is blessing or judgment.

Four leprous men at the gate reason that they will die either way, so they go over to the camp of the Syrians hoping to be spared. The Most High had made the host of the Syrians hear the noise of chariots and horses, so they fled in the twilight and left everything behind. The lepers eat and drink and carry off silver, gold, and raiment, hiding the spoil for themselves.

The lepers realize this is a day of good tidings and that they should not hold their peace, so they report to the king's household. The king suspects a trap, thinking the Syrians are hiding in the field to catch Israel coming out of the city. Messengers sent to investigate find the way to Jordan full of garments and vessels cast away in the Syrians' haste, and the people go out and spoil the tents, so the food is sold cheaply exactly as the word said.

The king sets the doubting lord in charge of the gate, and the people trod upon him there and he died, just as the man of God had spoken. The lord saw the plenty with his eyes but did not eat of it, so the word of the Most High fell out to the letter. The trampling in the gate stands as a picture of a crowd stampeding after goods, hating one another over things, and here it became the judgment on a man who doubted the word.

verses.text: Then Elisha said, Hear ye the word of the Lord; Thus saith the Lord, To morrow about this time shall a measure of fine flour be sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria.

Then a lord on whose hand the king leaned answered the man of God, and said, Behold, if the Lord would make windows in heaven, might this thing be? And he said, Behold, thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof.

For the Lord had made the host of the Syrians to hear a noise of chariots, and a noise of horses, even the noise of a great host: and they said one to another, Lo, the king of Israel hath hired against us the kings of the Hittites, and the kings of the Egyptians, to come upon us.
Wherefore they arose and fled in the twilight, and left their tents, and their horses, and their asses, even the camp as it was, and fled for their life.
And the people went out, and spoiled the tents of the Syrians. So a measure of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, according to the word of the Lord.

And the king appointed the lord on whose hand he leaned to have the charge of the gate: and the people trode upon him in the gate, and he died, as the man of God had said, who spake when the king came down to him.

And it came to pass as the man of God had spoken to the king, saying, Two measures of barley for a shekel, and a measure of fine flour for a shekel, shall be to morrow about this time in the gate of Samaria:

And that lord answered the man of God, and said, Now, behold, if the Lord should make windows in heaven, might such a thing be? And he said, Behold, thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof.
And so it fell out unto him: for the people trode upon him in the gate, and he died.
Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God.

And they rose early in the morning, and went forth into the wilderness of Tekoa: and as they went forth, Jehoshaphat stood and said, Hear me, O Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem; Believe in the Lord your God, so shall ye be established; believe his prophets, so shall ye prosper.
